---
title: "Method"
subtitle: "How I simulated, and what “normal enough” means in this study"
---



## The question behind the standard

The CLT is used to justify normal-based tools: 95% confidence intervals, margins of error, z- and t-tests.
All of them rest on one property of the normal curve: **2.5% of the probability lies beyond 1.96 standard
errors on each side**. So in this study, "approximately normal" means **normal enough that these tools
give nearly the right answer.** That purpose drives every threshold below.

## Monte Carlo design

| Element | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Sample size **n** | the quantity I am searching for | the size of one sample whose mean we study |
| Repetitions **B** | 100,000 sample means for every n | B sets how *precisely* each n is measured, not the answer; it costs seconds of computing |
| Seed | 9426 (last four digits of my student ID), set immediately before each n | each n is a self-contained, reproducible experiment, independent of which other n are tested |
| Search | coarse grid, then every n between the last failing and the first passing coarse n | the approach suggested in the assignment: start wide, then refine near the threshold |
| Code | one shared file, [`R/clt_functions.R`](https://github.com/JamV8/how-fast-does-normal-happen/blob/main/R/clt_functions.R), used by every analysis | every population is simulated and judged by exactly the same code |

## The four checks

| Check | What it measures | Ideal | Pass zone (main standard) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Skewness | asymmetry: is one tail longer? | 0 | between −0.25 and 0.25 |
| Excess kurtosis | are extreme values too common (+) or too rare (−)? | 0 | between −0.5 and 0.5 |
| Q-Q correlation r | how straight the normal Q-Q plot is | 1 | at least 0.998 |
| Tail check | share of sample means beyond μ ± 1.96·σ/√n, **each side separately** | 2.5% | between 1.75% and 3.25% on each side |

A sample size is **normal enough** when all four checks pass *and* the histogram and Q-Q plot show no
systematic departure from the normal curve. The chosen n is the smallest n that passes **and after which
every larger n I tested also passes**, so one lucky simulation cannot decide the answer.

Shapiro-Wilk p-values are reported but not used for decisions (see the last section).

## Why these thresholds

There is no universal cutoff, so I set each threshold between two limits:

1. **Not stricter than the simulation can measure.** Even perfectly normal data produce some nonzero
   skewness, kurtosis and tail error just by chance. A threshold must sit well above this noise.
2. **Not looser than practice can tolerate.** The threshold must keep the one-sided error rates of a 95%
   interval close to 2.5%.

### Limit 1: Monte Carlo noise


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show code: measuring the noise on truly normal data"}
set.seed(student_id)
noise <- replicate(200, {
  m <- rnorm(B)                       # B = 100,000 values that ARE normal
  c(skew(m), kurt(m), qq_cor(m), mean(m < -1.96), mean(m > 1.96))
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q correlation", "Each tail rate"),
  `Typical noise (SD over 200 runs)` = c(f3(sd(noise[1, ])), f3(sd(noise[2, ])),
                                        paste0("lowest of 200 runs: ", sprintf("%.5f", min(noise[3, ]))),
                                        pct(sd(c(noise[4, ], noise[5, ])), 2)),
  `Main threshold` = c("0.25", "0.5", "0.998", "2.5% ± 0.75%"),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrr")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Statistic       | Typical noise (SD over 200 runs)| Main threshold|
|:---------------|--------------------------------:|--------------:|
|Skewness        |                            0.008|           0.25|
|Excess kurtosis |                            0.015|            0.5|
|Q-Q correlation |      lowest of 200 runs: 0.99997|          0.998|
|Each tail rate  |                            0.05%|   2.5% ± 0.75%|


:::
:::


Each threshold is roughly ten times the noise or more, so a truly normal sampling distribution never fails
by chance. The kurtosis threshold is twice the skewness threshold because kurtosis is about twice as noisy.

### Limit 2: what skewness does to a 95% interval

If the sampling distribution has skewness γ, how often does the true mean fall beyond each end of the
usual ±1.96 SE interval? This can be computed exactly for gamma-shaped distributions, which have every
possible skewness:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show code: exact tail errors for a given skewness"}
tail_err <- function(g) {
  k <- (2 / g)^2                      # gamma shape with skewness g
  c(upper = pgamma(k + 1.96 * sqrt(k), k, lower.tail = FALSE),
    lower = pgamma(k - 1.96 * sqrt(k), k))
}
gs <- c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00)
te <- sapply(gs, tail_err)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Skewness = f2(gs),
  `Upper tail (should be 2.5%)` = pct(te["upper", ], 2),
  `Lower tail (should be 2.5%)` = pct(te["lower", ], 2),
  `Both tails (should be 5%)` = pct(colSums(te), 2),
  Verdict = c("nearly perfect", "**noticeable but acceptable (my main standard)**",
              "one side wrong by 2.5x", "unusable for one-sided tests"),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "rrrrl")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


| Skewness| Upper tail (should be 2.5%)| Lower tail (should be 2.5%)| Both tails (should be 5%)|Verdict                                          |
|--------:|---------------------------:|---------------------------:|-------------------------:|:------------------------------------------------|
|     0.10|                       2.77%|                       2.22%|                     4.98%|nearly perfect                                   |
|     0.25|                       3.14%|                       1.76%|                     4.91%|**noticeable but acceptable (my main standard)** |
|     0.50|                       3.68%|                       0.98%|                     4.66%|one side wrong by 2.5x                           |
|     1.00|                       4.47%|                       0.00%|                     4.47%|unusable for one-sided tests                     |


:::
:::


Two things follow:

- **0.25 is the compromise.** At 0.1 the intervals are almost perfect, but reaching it takes about
  (0.25/0.1)² ≈ 6 times more data. At 0.5 one side of the interval is wrong by a factor of 2.5. Halving the
  threshold multiplies the required n by four, because skewness shrinks as 1/√n.
- **The tails must be checked separately.** The *total* error barely moves (4.98% → 4.47%) even at
  skewness 1, because the two sides cancel. A two-sided tail check would pass a clearly skewed distribution.
  Checking each side against 1.75%–3.25% gives the same tolerance as skewness 0.25.

Kurtosis matters much less for 95% intervals: a symmetric distribution with excess kurtosis 0.5 puts about
5.2% instead of 5% outside ±1.96 SE. Kurtosis also fades quickly (as 1/n rather than 1/√n), so in practice
it acts as a safety net for heavy tails.

### Matching the Q-Q threshold to the skewness threshold


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show code: Q-Q correlation for a given skewness"}
set.seed(student_id)
gs2 <- c(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.50)
r_at <- sapply(gs2, function(g) mean(replicate(5, qq_cor(rgamma(B, shape = (2 / g)^2)))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Skewness = f2(gs2), `Average Q-Q r (B = 100,000)` = sprintf("%.5f", r_at),
                        check.names = FALSE), align = "rr")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


| Skewness| Average Q-Q r (B = 100,000)|
|--------:|---------------------------:|
|     0.10|                     0.99968|
|     0.15|                     0.99935|
|     0.20|                     0.99887|
|     0.25|                     0.99822|
|     0.30|                     0.99749|
|     0.50|                     0.99317|


:::
:::


A skewness of 0.25 corresponds to a Q-Q correlation of about 0.998, so I use **0.998**. My first draft
used 0.999. This check showed that 0.999 was secretly stricter than the skewness rule (it matches a
skewness of about 0.17), so the two rules contradicted each other. I corrected it.

## Three standards: a sensitivity analysis

Because the cutoff is a judgment call, I report every result under three standards that are calibrated the
same way. Only the main standard decides the chosen n.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|        |Standard | Max |skewness|| Max |excess kurtosis|| Min Q-Q r|     Each tail|
|:-------|:--------|------------------------:|-------------------------------:|---------:|-------------:|
|strict  |Strict   |                     0.10|                             0.2|    0.9996| 2.20% – 2.80%|
|main    |**Main** |                     0.25|                             0.5|    0.9980| 1.75% – 3.25%|
|lenient |Lenient  |                     0.50|                             1.0|    0.9930| 0.90% – 4.10%|


:::
:::


## Why I do not decide with Shapiro-Wilk

The Shapiro-Wilk test asks whether the data are *exactly* normal. With 5,000 points (its maximum in R) it
detects departures far too small to matter for a 95% interval:


::: {.cell}

:::


For the exponential population, 21 sample sizes passed all four of my checks, yet Shapiro-Wilk
still rejected normality (p < 0.05) at 20 of them, including n = 1,000
(p = 0.31). A test that answers "is it *perfectly* normal?" is the wrong tool
for "is it normal *enough*?", which is also the assignment's own warning.
